speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Chairman, I move, “That the total sum allocated to Head W of the Estimates be reduced by $100”.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Our connection to the world is imperative to our nation's relevance and economic vibrancy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As a small, open city‑state, Singapore's prosperity rests on strong links to other countries and global hubs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: To sustain that advantage, we must maintain state‑of‑the‑art air, sea and land nodes with the capacity and flexibility to handle current needs and future demand.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: To that end, Singapore is making significant, long‑term investments, as we have observed in Budgets past and present.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: These projects are designed to position Singapore as a continuing nexus for people, goods and information flows.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If delivered well, these projects will help Singapore attract capital, talent and advanced technology.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: More importantly, create new opportunities for our businesses and generate good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Improving lives must remain the ultimate objective of these investments.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Yet, we must also recognise these are multi-decade projects, consuming substantial public resources.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: They were planned in a different global environment that has become more volatile and uncertain.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Recent years have seen abrupt tariff barriers, supply chain restructuring and "hot wars" that disrupted energy and critical material supplies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Such shocks can re‑route trade and people flows, sometimes rapidly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Singapore will not be insulated from these shifts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Therefore, I have the following questions to raise.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Can we stage or modularise delivery so that we can accelerate to capture upside, or slow and recalibrate to limit downside?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: What contingencies are in place to manage cost escalation and preserve value for taxpayers?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Are we on track to capture near‑term opportunities, and where feasible, can delivery be accelerated without compromising quality, safety or long‑term flexibility?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Turning to our maritime sector specifically, capacity and connectivity, measured in twenty-foot equivalents (TEUs) and port calls, are critical determinants of competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: What economic impact does the Ministry project in terms of gross domestic product (GDP) contribution, value‑added services and the types of jobs and livelihoods it can create for Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In anticipation of these opportunities, what targeted programmes will be in place to cultivate and sustain a pipeline of maritime talent?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We must also prepare our infrastructure for the digital age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The Next‑Generation Port at Tuas is a good example.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Leveraging frontier technologies – automation, advanced sensors, predictive analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) – will keep our infrastructure globally competitive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But we must deploy technology responsibly to augment productivity while managing workforce transitions and reskilling needs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Hence, we must actively contemplate how technology should be leveraged to advance Singapore's connectivity and economic advantage.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: To this end, the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Transport plans to move a substantive Motion later this year, likely in July.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In closing, global connectivity is a strategic choice that must be actively maintained, future‑proofed and made inclusive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We should build fast enough and well enough to capture value, but also flexible enough to anticipate any macro-shocks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: At the same time, we must also always be prudent to adapt and protect public interest.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: It shapes how we work, learn, care for family and participate in our community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Over the years, our land transport system has become markedly more efficient, reliable and more integrated.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Heavy investment in public transport – expanding the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) network, modernising trains and signalling, upgrading bus fleets and developing integrated transport hubs just to name a few – has boosted capacity and improved connectivity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: These upgrades have made multimodal journeys smoother and helped shift commuters towards public and active modes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Looking ahead, technology advancement, demographic change and evolving lifestyles mean our land transport must continue to adapt.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Renewal and expansion therefore go hand in hand.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: What governance and funding approaches are in place to ensure upgrades are timely, cost‑effective and minimise commuter disruption during works?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Technology will reshape transport operations and service delivery.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: One certainty is a rise in electric vehicles (EVs) as we decarbonise; another is growing trials and deployments of Autonomous Vehicles (AVs).

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How is MOT coordinating with other agencies and industry to ensure sufficient power, standards for fast charging, and effective communications to support mass EV and AV adoption?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: As more technology is deployed, the transformation of land transport is something to look forward to.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: As sensors and connected systems, including increasingly intelligent EVs and AVs, share real time data, smart road and traffic management becomes feasible, enabling tighter coordination and more accurate traffic prediction.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: This should deliver smoother, more predictable journeys and materially improve the road user experience.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: On that note, an extensive deployment of AVs could significantly change vehicle population and ownership patterns.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: If AV fleets increase shared mobility and ride‑pooling, we may see pressure to reduce private car use.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Conversely, easier door‑to‑door transport could increase vehicle kilometres travelled.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How does MOT anticipate AV adoption affect the medium‑ to long‑term design of the COE system and other ownership controls?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Are there plans to recalibrate demand management, for example, differentiated measures for shared AV fleets versus privately owned vehicles?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I look forward to a land transport that anticipates future demands and is user centric.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: One with flexible infrastructure that can adapt to uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Technology effectively deployed to enhance commuter experience and demand management tools designed to reflect changing mobility patterns.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Sharael Taha, kindly deliver both your cuts together.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Singapore is assembling one of the world's most integrated aviation aerospace semiconductor logistics platforms.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But infrastructure alone does not create the advantage, ecosystems do.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Singapore can anchor high value functions, capital, intellectual property (IP), AI, finance and advanced manufacturing orchestration, while Johor and the Riau Islands can provide industrial scale and energy depth under the Sijori framework.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The national AI mission can be the force multiplier, enabling cross border smart factories, optimising multimodal flows, embedding trade finance, and strengthening regional medical and bio manufacturing supply chains.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The strategic question is how we elevate this infrastructure expansion into a coordinated AI-enabled economic engine that generates high value jobs, anchors capital and secures competitiveness for many decades in the East and Northeast districts in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And critically, how can MOT work hand in hand with the Ministry of Trade and Industry, the Ministry of Digital Development and Information, the Ministry of Manpower and the Ministry of Finance, and our regional counterparts to orchestrate, not just merely coordinate this ecosystem transformation at national scale?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As Singapore strengthens its position as a global logistics hub, I will seek clarification on three areas.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ultimately, growth must translate into good jobs, stronger skills and real opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Mr Chairman, when I became a pilot at 18, I was a minority because there were not too many women pilots in the Air Force.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Today, there are more of us, but we are still very much the minority, not just in the Air Force, but across the skies.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Mr Chairman, I must say that, from my experience as a search and rescue pilot, aviation as a career choice was the adventure of a lifetime and something I will not exchange for the world.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But it is also a very personal choice.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Hence, I target my speech not at setting a target or a quota of women in aviation, but as offering more opportunities and possibilities in our vibrant and world class air hub.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: First, I would like to ask for some figures.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: What is the representation of women in senior leadership in our aviation industry?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We know that it is very likely to be in the minority, but there is a large difference between 1% and 20%.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Second, I would like to offer some figures.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Global passenger traffic looks to double by 2040.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Aviation hubs in the region are now racing to increase their runway and terminal capacities, following the slowdown during the pandemic period.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But we are not only ones by a long shot.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Hong Kong International Airport is building its third runway.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: India, the world's most populous country, has built 75 new airports in the past decade and is set to build another 70 new airports soon.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: China will build more than 200 new airports by 2035.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Third, I would like to say what this means for us.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Given that the aviation sector is growing so quickly and that it is also very male dominant, what steps is MOT taking to attract talents, especially young women graduates in science, technology, engineering and mathematics.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Airline pilots, aeronautical engineers, ground hand operators, air traffic controllers, airport planners – there are many opportunities, many openings for young women, aviation professionals, and more women are taking up these roles recently.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: These are good jobs in the blue sky.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In the Asia Pacific region, Singapore has a conducive ecosystem to grow a strong network of women aviation professionals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We are leading Regional Aviation Hub with a thriving and well-connected airport, a major global air cargo hub, and a well-established MRO ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There are many jobs in these organisations, ranging from airlines, airports, cargo and logistics companies, as well as aircraft manufacturers and maintenance companies.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Of course, ensuring that women land well in aviation is not the work of Government alone.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: A culture shift is needed if we are to change from a male dominated working environment into a more inclusive one.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Considerations, such as the proper provision of basic amenities and facilities such as women's restrooms cannot be taken for granted.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In addition, human resources (HR) policies during pregnancy and maternity periods must also be well considered, as well as scholarship and internship opportunities.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Again, the Government does not have to do this alone.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There are groups in aviation, such as “Women Aviation International SG Chapter”, formed recently in 2021 to connect women professionals in aviation, providing mentoring support and offer scholarship opportunities.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Here, I declare my interest as an advisor to this organisation and an employee in the aviation industry.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: With an expanding industry and increased demand for skilled labour, the sky is the limit.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: For all of us, men and women who find their passion in aviation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Chairman, my Punggol residents are watching the autonomous shuttle pilots with keen interest.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: These trials are an important step in understanding how AV services may eventually integrate into our wider public transport ecosystem, particularly in strengthening first- and last-mile connectivity.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: At the same time, residents have practical questions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Will there be deeper engagements with different groups, including seniors, who may feel uncertain about travelling in AVs?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Adoption is not only about technology readiness, but public readiness.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: On the regulatory front, clarity is still needed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Will human operators or safety drivers be expected to bear responsibilities when system failures occur?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We must also be honest that the workforce implications remain unsettled, especially for our bus captain and point-to-point (P2P) drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We have yet to clearly define what new AV-related roles will look like, what fair compensation should be and how career pathways may evolve from today's driving and technical maintenance roles into future AV jobs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: As I had earlier highlighted in my Budget debate clarifications, while it is important for us to embrace new technologies, this must be done in a way that does not disrupt livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I therefore urge operators to work closely with our unions within our tripartite framework to co-create fair AV career pathways and ensure workers are supported through this transition.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Progress should strengthen both our public system and our people.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Chua, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, research and small scale testing of AVs for use on urban roads in Singapore has been going on for quite a while now.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With one of the earliest research and trials on the roads in one-north in partnership with nuTonomy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Another trial under the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) was started at one-north as well, sometime in 2014, this one under the Singapore Autonomous Vehicle Initiative.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In 2015, the MOT signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to further expand trials on AV with PSA Singapore and another with the Sentosa Development Corporation and ST Engineering, which I was lucky enough to experience myself.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There have been various other trials since then and fast forward to 2025, a 17-member committee chaired by the Acting Minister was formed to look at the roll-out of AVs on Singapore roads.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In comparison, in this time, the AV industry in places like China and the US has boomed, with their biggest players, Pony AI, WeRide and Waymo already running fully driverless commercial services in the cities they are operating in.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Pony AI aims for more than 3,000 vehicles by 2026, similar to WeRide.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Countries in the Middle East are also showing markedly faster implementation of AVs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Dubai Autonomous Transportation Strategy aims to have 25% of the total transportation in Dubai to be autonomous by 2030.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Saudi Arabia's Transport General Authority has set a target for 25% of all goods transport vehicles to be fully autonomous by 2030.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, according to SMRT, our public bus system is struggling to hire bus captains, especially from our local manpower pool.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: AVs as buses would ease the pressure on this issue, yet despite numerous trials all across the island.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's AV roll-out is still in the trial phase about 12 years on.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Beyond stating that Singapore will have, and I quote, "many autonomous vehicles in Singapore" in five years' time, can the MOT provide numerical targets for our AV ambition?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As my colleague Mr Gerald Giam shared more than a decade ago in 2015, Singapore is in an excellent position to lead the world in the adoption of driverless cars.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But we must ensure that legislation promotes and does not inhibit the test-bedding and public use of these vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope we will be able to accelerate AV roll-out in Singapore, especially for buses given the severe shortage of drivers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As part of Singapore's net-zero goal, Singapore aims to reduce land transport emissions and the electrification of vehicles is one of the key initiatives to help Singapore achieve this target.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One of the key pillars of the roadmap is the deployment of EV charging infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The vast majority, about 88%, are alternating current-based, of which about 50% have a low power rating of 7.4 kilowatts (kW) and below.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The majority of TotalEnergies' chargers, which represented 13% of Singapore's charging stations before they were taken over, are rated at 3.7 kW, which is the slowest among those accessible publicly, which take up to 16 hours to charge a typical EV.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Comparatively, only about 11% of chargers deployed have direct current, of which most of the DC chargers can qualify as "fast chargers".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Where typical AC chargers, typically take four to eight hours for a full charge, DC fast chargers can bring a battery to 80% in just 30 to 45 minutes, based on a May 2024 article by SP Group.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I wish to highlight however, that technology has advanced rapidly in this space.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In March 2025, BYD announced its super e-platform, which provides a 400-kilometre range in just five minutes of charging.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: BYD is now rolling out such megawatt level charging infrastructure in China.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For comparison, 1,000 kW is about one MW and this is 135 times higher vs the 7.4 kW typically found in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: LTA has already recognised that high-powered fast chargers will be needed to meet the needs of high-mileage users, particularly taxis and commercial fleets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Currently, it is typical for a Housing and Development Board (HDB) multi-storey car park to have only three slow chargers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We are now in February 2026 and while the "coverage" is higher, the "quality of access" remains unequal across our estates.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Ministry's primary defence for the current pace of scaling is that the average utilisation rate remains low.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, "average" utilisation is a misleading metric that may mask peak-hour reality.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For the HDB resident returning home at 9.00 pm, a low "average" rate is cold comfort when all three charging lots in their multi-storey car park are occupied.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: More crucially, we must scale up now for the eventuality that most vehicles in our carparks will be EVs – a goal we should strive to see earlier, in line with our 2030 and 2040 goals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If registrations continue to rise, when will "scaling up" reach all our heartland carparks?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And finally, how will MOT intend to mandate "idling fees" across all public charging operators to prevent lot-hogging?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Chairman, I would like to declare my interest as the CEO of Strides Premier, a company that leases out a fleet of more than 300 EVs, amongst other businesses.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: While the roll-out of slow chargers in HDB car parks has supported convenient overnight charging, many EV users, particularly P2P users as well as commercial drivers, require access to fast daytime charging infrastructure in the daytime so as to sustain their operations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I therefore urge LTA to spearhead the deployment of more fast chargers within the HDB estates, especially at convenient and high-traffic locations, such as near food establishments and neighbourhood centres.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, the rapid growth of EVs calls for a future-ready workforce.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Vehicle technicians must acquire new technical competencies to service EVs safely and effectively, supported by proper training and certification.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I encourage MOT to work closely with industry partners and training institutions to support technicians through this critical transition, ensuring our automotive workforce remains skilled, relevant and prepared for Singapore's electrified transport future.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some cyclists ring their bells persistently on crowded footpaths, as if expecting pedestrians to step off the path to make way for them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have personally experienced this and many of my residents have shared similar stories with me.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: LTA needs to reinforce that pedestrians always have the right of way.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Public education must clarify that bells should be used only to alert, not to demand a clear path.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must also educate pedestrians to keep left and avoid sudden changes in direction, for their own safety.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Residents frequently encounter cyclists zooming through bus stops, endangering passengers as they alight.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, those exiting lifts at their flats face risks from cyclists speeding past.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Why is there not more active education and enforcement of light requirements on footpaths?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, while footpaths next to cycling paths became pedestrian-only in July 2025, the converse is not true – pedestrians are not prohibited from walking on cycling paths.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If a dedicated pedestrian-only path exists, why is it not mandatory for pedestrians to use it?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will the Ministry reconsider a legal prohibition for pedestrians to use cycling paths, where a dedicated alternative is provided?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Though I thought driving him around would be ideal, I discovered that riding the bus was now a better option for some routes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our bus stops and buses are wheelchair friendly and the bus captains we met promptly got up from their seats to assist with the wheelchair platform.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such infrastructure and last-mile considerations go a long way to make travel accessible to the wheelchair-bound.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, mobility limitations come in a wide range.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Besides those on wheelchairs, there are many others who use walking sticks or other aids.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These commuters are often unable to navigate stairs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To what extent is our system barrier-free for them?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Take for instance the layout of some new electric buses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Increasingly, bus models appear to be designed to maximise standing room and space for wheelchairs and prams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This results in a reduction in the number of seats available.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In some buses, the front half of the bus only has four seats, with all the remaining seats located at the rear of the bus at an elevated level, requiring the commuter to climb a rather steep step.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This has caused difficulty to many commuters who can walk but cannot climb stairs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Ministry review how the layout of buses can better cater to commuters with such mobility issues?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another persistent issue is the lack of lifts at pedestrian overhead bridges.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is an issue across the island and it is also the case for my residents at the Paya Lebar Division of Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Two years later, in April 2025, I filed another question for confirmation of the bridges that would be prioritised and what the timeline for installation of the lifts would be.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is nearly two years after the fourth quarter of 2025 that Minister Chee indicated for commencement of that phase of construction works.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I hope to have a more satisfactory answer from the new Minister in charge.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Mr Chairman, I have filed this cut originally for the Ministry of National Development, but it was directed to MOT.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The vision of a car-light Singapore must require a seamless and sheltered first and last-mile experience for every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The Government has made meaningful progress, but more can be done.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The rear side gate links to an open footpath, which doubles as a covered drain and is heavily used by its residents, as it connects to the HDB covered linkway en-route to the nearest bus stop at Block 1, Hougang Avenue 3 – a few minutes walkaway.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: For the elderly and families with young children, this path is the most efficient way, yet poses challenges to them during heavy rains.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I wrote an appeal on the condominium's behalf to LTA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Attempts to request to construct the covered walkway have been challenging.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: While the land is under PUB, they do not build covered walkways.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Lastly, the Town Council has no jurisdiction to spend funds on projects that do not primarily benefit HDB residents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The request has been assessed primarily through agency boundaries rather than commuter experience.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This is a systemic no man's land problem.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Why should a resident's ability to reach public transport under cover depend on whether the ground or the drain beneath their feet is managed by HDB, LTA or PUB?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: If the goal is to encourage public transport usage and climate-proof our infrastructure, the last mile should be treated as a single continuous journey.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: To resolve such situations, I have three specific proposals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: First, can we institutionalise connectivity at the design stage?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: When the Riverfront Residences condominium at Hougang was built, the authorities allowed the developer to build covered linkways to the nearest bus stops.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This can be made a standard requirement where covered links are planned upfront and not added later as fixes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Third, can the Government assign a lead agency for connectivity?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: If a Management Corporation Strata Title is willing to pursue a walkway that serves a clear public connectivity purpose, the Government should provide a streamlined one-stop shop approach by an appointed agency for funding and approvals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This could be under URA, Building and Construction Authority or LTA.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, when my son goes to the army in the future, he will carry a 15-kilogramme Standard Battle Order every time he goes outfield.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, when I carry my 13-kilogramme son and his diaper bag onto public transport, I also feel like I am going outfield.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Once, when I was solo parenting, I almost tipped my son out of the stroller while trying to single-handedly board the bus with a stroller and the diaper bag.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many parents of young children have shared similar challenges navigating public transport safely and smoothly as a family.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Parents have also highlighted inconsistencies across operators, particularly on ramp deployment for strollers.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Boarding and alighting during peak hours remain difficult for parents and persons with disabilities, with limited space at stroller and wheelchair bays.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Supporting safe, smooth commutes is essential if Singapore is to be a home for families.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us lighten their load by making sure public transport is safe, accessible and supportive for families.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, during an MRT disruption last year, a deaf commuter shared that she felt confused and afraid when passengers began to leave the train as there were no visual or sign language updates explaining what was happening.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While initiatives such as the Sign Language Virtual Assistant SiLViA at Chinatown MRT station are encouraging, such support is not yet available across the network.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Could the Government update whether visual and sign language communication tools will be expanded so that disruption and emergency announcements are accessible to deaf commuters across our public transport system?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a Punggol resident, I speak from experience.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A 45-minute door-to-door journey to the city is for myself and most of my neighbours a pipe dream.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a city where housing comes at a premium, the families who live in Punggol, Sengkang, Woodlands and other far-flung towns have made pragmatic choices about where to put down roots.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Every morning, they pay for that choice in time.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not have a two-speed Singapore where time is a privilege of the few.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To understand what happens when ambition falls short, we need to look no further than the North East Line (NEL).

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My fellow Members and I have filed multiple Parliamentary Questions on the NEL's capacity crisis over the months.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Solutions to the crisis are in short supply.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Longer trains would require excavation works that would disrupt the line for over a year.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Selective door operation has been studied and rejected.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even at maximum peak frequency, commuters at Hougang and Kovan watch full trains pass them by.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Residents in the North-East have become resigned to long crowded commutes.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We built a NEL without the headroom to grow it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Seletar Line gives us a chance to do better.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2018, express services were studied for the Cross Island Line and rejected on cost-benefit grounds.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But a point-in-time cost-benefit calculation is the wrong basis for infrastructure that has to serve multiple generations.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Seoul, their Metro Line 9 faced identical scepticism of their express service.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The time to make this decision is during current feasibility studies and not after ground-breaking, and certainly not after the line is in operation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The least we can do is to bring them back to the city at speed.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge the Ministry to plan the Seletar Line with the foresight that the NEL lacked and the ambition that the next generation of Singapore deserves.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: It will connect to Woodlands North MRT station on the Thomson-East Coast Line.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: It may soon be a $5 to $7 ticket to a place of good bargains and family outings.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Many of my residents in Sembawang West are looking forward to the RTS.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Some have relatives in Johor, many go over to do their grocery shopping, for family trips and simple services such as haircuts, spectacles, dental treatment and facials.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: But for every change, there will be ripples.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: There will be more Singaporeans using the Thomson-East Coast Line.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: At the same time, we have already read in newspaper reports that Malaysian workers who used to rent in Singapore now may move back and take RTS to work in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: At $10 commute a day, this may work out economically against the rentals and spending in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: We do want people to use the line and my prediction is that under-demand will not be a problem.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Due to these increases in movements, the morning peak period at Woodlands North station and the traffic on the Thomson-East Coast Line may see a massive surge.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Does the Minister have an update on how much the fares will actually cost?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Many Malaysians work in the semiconductor and food manufacturing factories located within the Woodlands industrial area.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Instead of renting a room here, the workers may choose to commute via RTS and cycle or walk two kilometres to their workplaces.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Does LTA have plans to widen the shared paths used also by the residents to better cope with the potential increase in cycling and pedestrian traffic?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Chairman, I would like to declare that I am the CEO of Strides Premier, a subsidiary of SMRT.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: MRT remains the backbone of our public transport system, shaping how Singaporeans live, work and connect.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Across the island, residents are eagerly waiting for the next phase of rail expansion.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Residents and businesses are looking forward to the long-awaited closure of the Circle Line loop.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: This critical interchange will significantly strengthen network resilience and provide commuters with more reliable travel options.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Chairman, in the West, anticipation for the Jurong Region Line (JRL) is especially strong.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: For many families in Nanyang and across Jurong, this line represents shorter commutes and better access to jobs and amenities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Residents along Jurong West Street 91 live near the future Gek Poh MRT station, yet it is beyond walking distance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How will we balance necessary service closures against commuter inconvenience?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: What concrete contingency plans will minimise hardship and what guaranteed service levels such as standby buses, response time and fair consideration will commuters be assured of?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How are we strengthening supply chain resilience for critical rail components?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Beyond hardware, how are we building engineering depth, sharpening recovery protocols and ensuring real-time commuter information is accurate, timely and actionable?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Mr Chairman, my first cut on rail development.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Chairman, as we continue strengthening our rail network, we must recognise that human capital is key to building a resilient and reliable rail ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: With parts of our network ageing, including lines, assets and equipment, renewal and upgrading works will intensify.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In this context, I would like to seek updates on what rail workers can expect in terms of fair competitive remuneration packages, training and safer workplaces.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: We appreciate that under the Rail Safety Report, there will be moves towards harmonised training for rail technicians.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Today, there remains significant localisation across rail systems in maintenance practices, equipment and repair processes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Without harmonisation, workers' skills become tied to one system, one line or one operator.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: While operators are given flexibility to deploy this grant, how can we ensure that its impact reaches a broader segment of all rail workers?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: For example, could sector-level key performance indicators be considered, such as equipping 50% of workers with new competencies by 2030?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: How can we better protect rail workers from verbal abuse or confrontation when they carry out these duties?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: A strong rail ecosystem depends not only on modern assets, but on a skilled and protected workforce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As the Bus Contracting Model marks its 10th year, it is timely for us to review how it is working – not just for operational efficiency, but for our bus captains.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: They remain the backbone of our public transport system.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: This raises an important question: are we building a sustainable profession or one where earnings depends on longer hours?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: If we want to maintain a strong Singaporean core, we must relook bus captains pay, working conditions and career progression.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Today, captains manage split shifts, short meal breaks, long hours, fatigue, changing commuter patterns and increasingly difficult commuter behaviours.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: With the rise of social media, they are also increasingly vulnerable to online harassment and doxxing when incidents are recorded and circulated.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: What more can be done to better protect their safety at work?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Are our current training pathways sufficient to prepare bus captains for this transition?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: At the same time, with revenue bus AV services expected to begin in the second half of this year, we must ensure that affected workers are supported with clear career pathways and fair packages.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: We have seen how the Rail Manpower Development Package supports rail workers through change.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As the Bus Contracting Model (BCM) enters its next phase, could a similar transformation support be considered for our bus captains?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: A refreshed BCM should be a win-win for commuters, operators and the workers who keep Singapore moving.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: While the Government has repeatedly cited the 400-metre benchmark and the availability of 14 bus services in the vicinity, this technical standard does not fully capture the lived reality of our residents, particularly our elderly and persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Simultaneously, we are building a more inclusive society that recognises the needs of persons with physical disabilities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: For these residents, even a 400-metre walk is not merely inconvenient.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Seniors with reduced mobility, persons using wheelchairs or walking aids, those recovering from medical procedures and individuals managing chronic conditions may find this distance insurmountable, especially in our tropical heat.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The distinction between technical accessibility and practical accessibility matters profoundly.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: In practice, vulnerable residents face daily challenges that prevent them from accessing essential services, healthcare and community activities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Extending Bus 371 would increase journey times for existing commuters.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: However, I urge the authorities to explore creative solutions, perhaps introducing a new short loop feeder service that connects Compassvale Crescent directly to Sengkang MRT – without affecting existing routes or a community shuttle service piloted specifically for those with mobility challenges, our Bus Connectivity Enhancement Programme should embody our national values of inclusivity and care for vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: It enables independence, dignity and full participation in society.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I therefore renew my call for LTA to reconsider this matter, focusing not on whether residents can technically access buses, but whether our transport network truly serves all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Chairman, during elections, I campaigned on supporting the sandwiched generation, promoting sustainability and empowering our youths.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But my residents in Pasir Ris-Changi have made me deeply passionate about something else – our land transport system.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: On paper, low ridership data may appear insufficient to justify new services or increased frequency.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But I would like to argue that retrospective data does not capture suppressed demand.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Many residents have grudgingly shifted their commute behaviour to costlier, more pollutive means that worsens road congestions because they feel there is no reliable public transport alternative.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My first suggestion is this: can the Ministry move beyond relying heavily on retrospective ridership data when refining bus service plans?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I urge the Ministry to survey residents directly and leverage community feedback, to unlock real rider demand.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: When public transport options are limited or unreliable, more residents turn to private vehicles.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This adds pressure to already busy roads, such as Loyang Avenue.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: During the recent Land Transport Bill debate, I spoke about our Pasir Ris resident Mrs Malar Singam, who was seriously injured by a power-assisted bicycles rider last December.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While regulations have been strengthened, more can be done to clearly segregate paths so that our seniors, like Malar, are kept safe.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Residents have requested stronger enforcement and speed cameras at specific locations.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Yet enforcement remains inconsistent and cameras have not been installed where risks have been reportedly highlighted.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Can the Ministry then share what alternative enforcement measures have been implemented to make this road safer?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Real-time noise monitoring systems are already in place.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My request is that enforcement be equally real-time.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Contractors who exceed limits should face prompt consequences and not action only after complaints.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Many residents in the area are also disturbed by the noise of illegally modified motorcycles late at night, many involving foreign-registered vehicles.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And have we worked with the Ministry of Manpower to explore whether repeated violations could carry Work Pass consequences?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is no longer confined to peak hours or the Central Business District.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Heavy traffic is now common even on weekends, along arterial roads and across our expressway network.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Road accidents and ongoing works further compound delays, affecting not just motorists but also bus commuters and private-hire passengers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I hope that this is not the response later.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I therefore urge the Ministry not to look to non-pricing approaches as well to manage congestions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With over a million vehicles on our small island, higher vehicle utilisation appears to be one of the root cause for the congestions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The growth of private-hire services and delivery platforms has intensified road usage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As car ownership becomes more expensive, owners understandably want to maximise usage of their cars, because of sunk costs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Given these structural trends, we should explore complementary solutions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Compared to underground tunnels, such solutions may be more cost-efficient and faster to implement.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With limited land for widening, vertical expansion may be our most feasible option in certain corridors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, does the Ministry have plans to develop more double-tier road systems in congestion-prone areas?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And are there plans for additional multi-level interchanges at heavily congested junctions?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Beyond capacity expansions, small but targeted engineering refinements can yield significant gains – improved slip-road geometry, better lane merging designs and additional turning lanes at bottlenecks.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The growth of e-commerce has increased delivery traffic substantially.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Logistics vans, service vehicles and contractor trucks contribute to daytime congestions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can we encourage off-peak delivery windows in dense commercial districts?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And can we also expand urban consolidation centres to reduce duplicate trips, or promote shared last-mile distribution hubs to improve logistical efficiency?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Minor accidents often trigger cascading congestion, especially on expressways.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The speed of detection and clearance is critical.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can we station more rapid-response tow units along major corridors to expeditiously clear stalled vehicles?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: During accidents, many motorists still have this old belief that vehicles should not be moved until the Police arrive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In today's context, with in-car cameras and mobile devices readily available, this is often unnecessary.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Instead, we should consider requiring drivers in minor, non-injury accidents to clear the carriageway within a fixed timeframe after documenting the incident, for example, just in 10 minutes, and with enforcement actions for unreasonable delays.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Motorists often encounter red lights even when cross-direction traffic appears light or if there are no vehicles travelling.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While adaptive systems are in place, signal timings do not seem to be responsive or smart.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can we move towards more advanced AI-based signal optimisation?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: A more dynamic and predictive system could reduce stop-start traffic and improve traffic throughput.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Some cities are already using fairly advanced computing technologies, such as quantum technologies, to enhance traffic management.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Is the Ministry looking into that as well?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition to physical and technological interventions, behavioural nudges may help.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Providing more granular, real-time congestion data integrated into navigation platforms may encourage voluntary route changes or staggered departures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Also, flexible work arrangements, through inter-agency coordination, could also help flatten peak demand.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And all these suggestions that I have made, I hope would also help to reduce congestions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I look forward to the Ministry's reply, outlining fresh and forward-looking non-pricing strategies to manage congestion.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: But one persistent challenge remains: the misalignment of responsibility in road traffic incidents.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Too often, when collisions or infractions occur, public discourse frames fault as lying solely with "others" – the reckless driver, inconsiderate cyclist or distracted pedestrian.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: This mindset risks obscuring the reality that safe mobility is a shared responsibility.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Pedestrians, cyclists, motorists and transport planners each have a role in ensuring that our roads functions safely for everyone.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, this policy cut is intended to encourage a deeper, more systemic conversation about how we share responsibility for road safety, recognising that blaming "others" alone is not sufficient to drive meaningful behaviour change.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, I will speak on three areas: one, ERP 2.0 resulting in increasing of vehicular supply; two, refreshing the Certificate of Entitlement (COE) system for greater equity; and three, accessibility in car ownership in our next phase of land transport policy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During the Land Transport Bill debate, I highlighted that ERP 2.0 presents an opportunity to move beyond congestion pricing and towards smarter traffic optimisation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By harnessing more granular real-time data, we can integrate ERP insights with adaptive traffic systems such as intelligent traffic signals, and guide infrastructure planning and network adjustments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If supply increases, more families who need a car for caregiving needs can gain access to one.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The key issue is not whether vehicle numbers should increase, but whether any adjustments are tied to measurable congestion outcomes and communicated clearly.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Optimisation must strengthen traffic flows and policy confidence.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, refreshing the COE system for greater equity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The original intent of the COE classification was equity, differentiating between mass-market and higher-end vehicles.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Manufacturers are adjusting specifications, whether engine power or motor design, so that premium models qualify under Category A (Cat A), while practical vehicles end up in Category B (Cat B) due to technical criteria, even though they are not luxury vehicles.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This shows that higher-end cars can fall into Cat A, while practical models fall under Cat B, undermining the original intent to distinguish mass-market from luxury.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Technical thresholds no longer reliably reflect affordability or market positioning.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The price delta between Cat A and Cat B is also narrowing, signalling reduced meaningful differentiation between the categories.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, in the recent COE bidding exercise, Cat A premiums exceeded Cat B.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This raises questions about whether the current framework still achieves its intended segmentation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If equity remains the policy objective, we should ask whether engine capacity and power output remain the right measures.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, OMV provides a stronger basis for differentiation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It reflects the true purchase cost of a vehicle rather than technical specifications alone.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We already use OMV to calculate Additional Registration Fee (ARF) through a tiered structure.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Pooling supply into one category will smooth out price fluctuations caused by mismatches in supply and demand between categories.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As our society ages and more families support members with disabilities or special needs, mobility becomes a necessity and not just a convenience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While the COE framework focuses on congestion management, we should consider calibrated mechanisms that support genuine caregiving needs without undermining system integrity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such an approach offers a clearer and more transparent way to achieve accessibility objectives compared to introducing additional special categories, which can become complex to define and administer.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, ERP 2.0 allows us to better optimise our limited land resource and may enable calibrated increases in vehicle supply, giving more families access to mobility.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Refreshing the COE framework by anchoring differentiation on OMV provides clearer distinctions between mass-market and luxury vehicles; while tiered adjustments can enhance accessibility for families with caregiving needs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In doing so, we preserve market discipline while strengthening fairness and accessibility in car ownership.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Chairman, I would like to declare my interest as the CEO of Strides Premier.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: This marks the first decline since 2025 and appears to contradict the earlier position stated by the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I would therefore like MOT to clarify whether there has been a change in policy direction, and if so, the reasons behind this shift.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In the second bidding exercise of February, Cat A COE price was even higher than the Cat B COE price by $1,500.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In the first bidding exercise in March, which just ended, the gap is also quite narrow between the Cat A and Cat B COE at $5,782.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: This convergence may also be driven by market developments, including the growing ease of tuning EVs to meet Cat A criteria, as well as the increasing presence of higher-end internal combustion engine vehicles with lower engine capacities qualifying under Cat A .

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: If the trend of declining Cat A COE supply and rising Cat B COE supply continues, the convergence of Cat A and Cat B COE prices will persist.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Such an outcome would run contrary to the original intent of maintaining distinct categories within the passenger car segment.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: As MOT has previously stated, the primary objective of Cat A COE is to preserve a portion of the vehicle quota for mass-market cars, thereby ensuring greater accessibility and affordability for the average Singaporean car buyer.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I would therefore like MOT to clarify whether there has been any shift in this policy intent and if so, the reasons for the shift.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Chairman, many residents have shared with me their frustrations over the persistently high COE prices.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: At different stages of life, some Singaporeans may have a greater need for a car than others, such as families with young children and those caring for elderly parents, or salespersons whose livelihoods depend on mobility.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I therefore hope the Ministry will continue to keep these Singaporeans in mind and ensure that our policies remain fair and balanced.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This influx indicates that motorcycles owned by Singaporeans are not the source of congestion.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The traffic issues we face are not stemming from motorcycles, yet the COE imposes a financial burden on those who purchase them.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Typically, buyers of motorcycles of lower- and middle-income earners who rely on these vehicles for work, including roles in delivery services.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Penalising them with the COE is unjust, especially when they do not contribute to traffic congestion.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Removing the COE for motorcycles would alleviate financial strain and allow these individuals to save money, ultimately enabling them to generate more income and improve their livelihoods.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Mr Chairman, first of all, let me give my thanks to Members for the very thoughtful cuts.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: As I was listening to the speeches, I felt grateful for the many good suggestions and ideas from colleagues in the Chamber.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I do not think we will be able to address every single idea and question today that has been asked of us, but we will try.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: It is a long-standing tradition that MOT has many cuts.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I should know because I used to work there as a civil servant. "Death by a thousand cuts," as we used to say.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But the interest, your interest shows just how much transport is part of Singaporeans daily lives.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Every morning, millions of people step out of their homes and trust that the system will work.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: When transport works well, it becomes part of our routines, but when it does not, it affects your jobs, your family time, your peace of mind.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: It is a privilege for us to work on issues that matter so much to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Singaporeans are connected to the world by air, and most of what we eat, buy and use is brought to us by sea.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: What happens elsewhere in the world can therefore affect us significantly, and this includes the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which we are watching very closely.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: As the world around us becomes more volatile, we need to strengthen the foundations that allow Singapore to survive and thrive.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: International rules and standards are critical for both aviation and maritime, which operate across national borders.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: And to shape these rules and standards, Singapore has served on the councils of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and the International Maritime Organization (IMO) for over two decades.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Last year, my team and I campaigned for re-election to both councils.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I was moved by the strong support that other countries expressed for Singapore.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: They appreciated our solid record of leadership, consensus building and spearheading training programmes over the years.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: At the same time, it was evident that the rules-based global order is under strain.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Consensus at ICAO and IMO is harder to achieve, especially on long-term issues like sustainability.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: And we are seeing more factions along lines of national interest, instead of global benefit.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: To bolster our influence abroad, we draw from our strength at home.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Our air and sea hubs are both world-class.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Changi Airport is one of the best airports in the world; and PSA International is one of the world’s most successful port operators.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling asked about the latest developments for T5 and Tuas Port.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: As Ms Poh Li San noted, this will increase Changi’s capacity by about 50 million passengers per year.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Looking at passenger growth trends, we are confident this capacity will be needed to meet underlying demand.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The completion of T5 will also open up the possibility of remaking the older terminals, T1 to T4, in the future.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked about the broader aviation ecosystem that will complement T5.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Indeed, the ecosystem we are building goes beyond the terminal itself, to the Changi East Industrial Zone, the Changi East Urban District and potentially, the Tanah Merah Ferry Terminal for better air-sea connectivity.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: This aerotropolis, to borrow Mr Sharael’s term, will be sustainable and technology-intensive, and will create many good jobs, while better serving passengers, air cargo users and MRO companies.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Senior Minister of State Murali will share more.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: These major infrastructure projects are only possible because of our Government’s focus on long-term planning.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We started planning for T5 13 years ago and Tuas Port almost 30 years ago.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: When we design these projects, we are not just thinking about today.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: This is why I am happy to hear that Ms Tin Pei Ling and the GPC for Transport will file a Motion on the deployment of technology in transport later this year.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I look forward to another exciting debate on the future of transport then, in a few months.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: For MRT lines, we also plan far ahead.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I heard the requests from Ms Poh Li San, Mr Ang Wei Neng, Mr Andre Low and Mr Sharael Taha for updates on various MRT projects.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: An MRT line takes about 15 years to build.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: And in just 20-over years, we have almost doubled the length of our entire MRT network.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The two lines will be connected at Sungei Bedok station.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Later this year, we will also open Circle Line Stage 6, so the Circle Line will finally be a real circle.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Next year, we plan to start construction on the Cross Island Line Phase 3, which will extend the line from Jurong Lake District westwards.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I also promised Mr Ng Chee Meng an update on the Seletar and Tengah Lines.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We plan to commence engineering studies this year.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Mr Ng’s residents would be happy to know that we will prioritise studying a corridor to serve Sengkang West and Serangoon North.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: This could also include future connections to the Cross Island and Circle Lines.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The first phase of the extension will connect the JRL to the Cross Island Line.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: LTA has started works for a new JRL station, between Tengah and Choa Chu Kang stations.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The working name of the station is JS2a – very unimaginative, because the last time we tried to be imaginative, it is very hard to change people's minds when we have to move the station.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: So, JS2a is targeted to open in the mid-2030s and will serve residents in the Forest Hill district in Tengah, in time for the completion of housing developments there.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The JRL was planned to open in end-2027.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Many of my residents, especially in Tengah, are looking forward to it, because it will be a game-changer for their transport options.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I know some of my residents, who have already moved into Tengah, will be disappointed.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But we will do our best to complete the works as soon as possible.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Ms Poh Li San asked for an update on the RTS Link.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: This is another long-term project that took years of discussion with Malaysian counterparts.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The economic case for the RTS Link is clear.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But the project still required sustained commitment from both Governments.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We have planned the capacity of the Thomson-East Coast Line such that it is more than sufficient to accommodate the passenger numbers arriving via the RTS Link.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Ms Poh asked about the fares for the RTS Link.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I know my counterpart in Malaysia has announced a figure of $5-$7.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I have not discussed the fares with him.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But under the terms of our Bilateral Agreement, it is the operator, RTS Operations Pte Ltd (RTSO), who has to determine the fares.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We await RTSO’s announcement of fares in due course.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Announcing new MRT lines is even more exciting.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But just as important is to maintain the system that is already built.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The oldest part of our MRT network – the North-South and East-West lines – is close to 40 years old now.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: And I was reminded of this last year, when we retired the last of our first generation MRT trains – the Kawasaki-C151s.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Many people of my vintage would have fond memories of taking these trains as a child for the first time when the MRT was first built.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I have a photo that I treasure very deeply because it is a photo of me and my father taking the train for the first time.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: It is timely to rejuvenate some of our older, well-loved MRT stations as well, not just for trains.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: For instance, we announced last year that we will rejuvenate Yishun MRT station, with a new entrance, additional lifts and a larger concourse.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: LTA is now studying other stations for rejuvenation, including Admiralty, Khatib and Sembawang.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Beyond our MRT network, we are also planning for a future with AVs.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The technology has taken awhile to mature, but with advances in AI, sensors, mapping and computing, AVs are finally a reality.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Recently, we have been deploying AVs quite aggressively in closed environments like our airport and seaport, for baggage and cargo.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But it will be some time yet before we see mass deployment of autonomous passenger vehicles on our roads.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: After all, there are fewer than 7,000 such AVs in the world today, a tiny fraction of the total vehicle population here in Singapore.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: What we are doing now though is to plan ahead and prepare early, as we have always done.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We have been trialling AVs in Punggol since last September, to learn how AVs can work in Singapore’s context.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Since January, we have been taking passengers on the AVs, by invitation.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The AV trials have been running smoothly and safely, and many Punggol residents have expressed strong support.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: They have been asking Senior Minister of State Sun Xueling and me, whether they can start taking rides on the AVs, and when.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: So, I am happy to announce that from 1 April, we will open up rides for interested members of the public.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Not an April Fools' joke; 1 April, we will open up rides for interested members of the public.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Rides will be free for a short period, before we begin revenue service.
