text: So, I would like to understand whether it is possible to give us a sense of how such costs may increase over time, both the construction and lifetime maintenance, and whether it is feasibly sustainable over the longer run.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: If yes or no, how are we going to manage this?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Chairman, I will take the first question and I will have Minister of State Baey take the second one.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We will take it as part of the Land Transport Master Plan process as Minister of State Baey has explained.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: As Ms Tin has mentioned, with the changing needs of the population, our infrastructure needs to keep up with the needs.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We are now focusing on locations that serve more seniors.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We may need a few years, because as we have mentioned in the House before, construction of a pair of lifts at the POB is not so straightforward.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We need to look at underground services that may be disrupted and various things.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The Member has rightly pointed out, it is not just building it, it is also maintaining the lifts subsequently.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: After Phase 4, do we have Phase 5 and subsequent phases?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We do have Members asking for lifts at POBs in their respective areas.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I believe, if I am not wrong, we have easily more than 700 POBs around Singapore.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I do not think we will be able to install lifts at all the POBs or, in that argument or rationale, improve amenities or infrastructure to cater to all needs of the population over time.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I think MOT and LTA will have to look at each of the request and come up with a strategy of addressing the needs of as many as commuters as quickly as possible, as I have mentioned in my speech.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: It is about balancing the different needs, managing our resources prudently, bearing in mind not only the cost of the construction development but the whole tail of maintenance.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We will definitely make sure that whatever we build will be maintained properly.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We call to the public and commuters to make use of these facilities properly, make sure that they last a long time so that we do not need to do repairs or refurbishment too frequently.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I believe that with that kind of approach, we will be able to cater to the needs of our ageing population in time to come.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There are a number of POBs in my division as well, Minister of State Baey.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In the meantime, I would like to seek clarification on the reduction in the supply of Category A COE.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: If so, could MOT consider rebalancing the supply of Cat A and B COE, using the new allocation, at least for the next 12 months.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: This approach will help to moderate the price of Cat A COE while waiting for MOT's review of criteria for Cat A and Cat B COE, which Minister has said will take until the end of the year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: We would like to enquire whether MOT will increase the subsidies for the public transport to ensure that these measures do not result in higher transport fares?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We have been doing it based on a certain methodology that involves redistributing guaranteed de-registrations via cut and fill, as well as then subsequently doing the injections.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The objective is to smoothen the COE quota supply overall.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As to whether we want to inject another parameter, which is to rebalance Cat A and B, we will evaluate that, but I am hesitant about introducing too many parameters.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Because, as I think one of the Members, I think it was Mr Edward Chia, who said that in the course of doing this, we do not want to add too much uncertainty, too many variables and therefore, too much perturbation to the market.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, we will evaluate it, but I think, just sort of thinking offhand, probably not too likely.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: On the second question on the bus captains, we are discussing with the unions as well as with the bus operators on how to execute the increase in the salaries for new recruits, starting salaries of bus captains.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And I think Government is prepared to see what we can do to put in more support to the system.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But I wish to point out that, in fact, for the bus network, the Government has already put in a lot of resources to support the financial sustainability of the bus network.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I mentioned the Bus Connectivity Enhancement Programme, which is a significant inject of funds.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We have to see then overall, how the fiscal sustainability of the bus network can be maintained, so that we can continue to grow the network at a sustainable pace and that salaries are also then incorporated into the overall cost of maintaining this network.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: So, can I ask the Minister to consider again what I have raised in the cuts, which is that can we optimise the traffic light system, something that many countries have done; and how we can make it more responsive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: It could be a really a good high-value AI-use case.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: And then, the second suggestion, I mentioned about how we can have more expeditious clearing of vehicles during accidents.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: It is not really a high infrastructure item, something that can be managed, can be done.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: You just need to have the policy in place to say, "You got to clear the traffic within a certain time and there must be enough tow vehicles", and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: So, I hope the Minister can give me a more encouraging response.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: First of all, I want to apologise to Mr Liang Eng Hwa because he made a wonderful speech on transport with many ideas.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And I was unable to reply to all the ideas that he had put out.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But as he asked the clarification, it gives me an opportunity to be able to respond more fully to the good ideas that he has suggested.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The answer is: not to worry, ERP is not our first option by any means.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: On using technology, I think Mr Liang gave many examples and I agree with him that, in fact, using AI for systems, such as traffic light management, would significantly improve the fluidity of our traffic.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And in fact, the LTA is exploring this.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: They showed me something recently, has a very nice acronym called CRUISE.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I do not know what it stands for, but it looks reasonable and I am happy to find a time to share with Mr Liang, if he is interested.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: There were a few other suggestions on, for example, double deck highways on Keppel.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think that is less likely something that we will do.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I am reminded of Boston, a city which had I spent quite a bit of time in.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: They had this Big Dig – I do not know whether you would be familiar with it.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: They spent many years and vast amounts of money putting that two double decker highway into the ground.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And today, if you go to Boston, it is a much nicer place to be in, and we have all, as a student, I have driven on that before.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I can tell you, it was not a pleasant experience, and more importantly, it bifurcated the sea front from the city.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, I do not think we really want to do that as far as possible here.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Very much so, we will work with the industry to try to improve how we do logistics in Singapore, make it smoother, in terms of delivering goods.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: In fact, MOT and MTI have been coming together to try to develop a logistics strategy that is more coherent.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And I think at the appropriate time we will update the House on this.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Actually, the Expressway Monitoring and Advisory System (EMAS) already does quite a good job.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Usually, after they clear the accident, if it is a minor accident, it takes about maybe half an hour to an hour for traffic to get back to normal.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But for a serious accident, where if it involves a fatality, it needs a bit more time, and that is when the more difficult jams happen.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, I think in terms of performance, it is already not bad, but I agree with Mr Liang that we should use technology to see how we can speed up those processes and reduce the impact of such incidents.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I see a more encouraged look from Mr Liang now.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Just one clarification for Ministers on the EV chargers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I think the MOT has previously said that we are looking at three to 12 charging points per HDB carpark by 2025, but my question is not so much on the deadline, but more in terms of the number of chargers that can be supported, because in most of the multi-storey car park that I see, it is typically just three 7.4 kilowatt chargers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: So, I just wondering in terms of the original tenders that were put out to upgrade the electricity infrastructure, what was the maximum power capacity or number of charging stations that can be supported?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, moving forward, we are monitoring developments in charging technology, and that is why in my speech, I had talked about a mix of slow chargers as well as fast chargers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I wanted to take the opportunity to talk about how we are sequencing our fast-charging hubs.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I had mentioned that we will be looking at having one in each HDB town, and this will be relying on existing spare capacity at car parks where possible, and for future tranches of deployment, we are also working with the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI), and the Energy Market Authority (EMA) to optimise our electrical grid to minimise costly grid upgrades.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, I think when we look at our charging infrastructure, we should look at it holistically.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It should be a mix in future of slow chargers, fast chargers, and we are keeping our eye on ultra-fast charging hubs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Just want to confirm that he mentioned that it could also be based on the OMV system, but there will also be considerations on combining into a single pool, doing away with Cat A and Cat B?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Can I confirm if that it is also under consideration?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Second, also, in terms of the consultation exercise, could you share who are the usual stakeholders that will be involved in the consultation exercise?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: My second clarification is to Senior Minister of State Sun.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: I think she mentioned about fast charging points, one per HDB town, and I think she mentioned that there will be six charging points per town.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: But typically, a HDB town has about 10,000 to 12,000 vehicles.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Just want to check what is the projection in terms of adequacy, I think she mentioned about working with JTC and EMA to improve, what are the current limitations and what are the plans to actually resolve this limitation, so we can scale up more fast charging points per HDB town?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: And my third clarification is to Senior Minister of State Murali, very pleased to hear that the maritime sector offers great job opportunities for Singaporeans and congratulations to the young scholars in Chamber today.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Just want to ask what are the further plans to create more awareness among young Singaporeans about the job opportunities within the maritime sectors and in particular, what is current take-up rate for the GRaduate Industry Traineeships (GRIT) programme?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: And are there scopes to scale up the GRIT programme, so that more young Singaporeans can be exposed to the maritime sector and seize these opportunities for themselves?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I will take Mr Chia's first question, and then I will have the two Senior Ministers of State reply to his subsequent two questions.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think we have to look at how to do this, because there is probably still some merit to having some distinction between a mass market car category and a higher-end car category.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We have to see how we can do this, but I think his idea is a very interesting one and we are very happy to try to explore that in the context of trying to find a system of categorisation that is a little bit more stable in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As to who we consult, we will consult a range of stakeholders, obviously car buyers, both potential and current car users.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We also want to consult the industry, so this would include both the motor dealers, but also car manufacturers and other industry observers.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think we will also consult academics as well, because in a system like the COE, it involves auctions and I suppose, auction theory is very well developed.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: It is something that the academics will have something to say; and we will be very happy to seek views from them as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: On the specific issue about the GRIT programme, that involves traineeship, the good thing about the maritime sector is that we have jobs available.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As to what further things we can do, I have identified in my speech, we work very closely with stakeholders, such as the Singapore Maritime Foundation, IHLs, our tripartite partners, our unions as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And just one example that underscores this point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I spoke not too long ago about this lady, Ms Valerie Thai, who was a paralegal in a law firm.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: She attended an exhibition in a shopping mall that was run by the Singapore Maritime Officers' Union and the Employment and Employability Institute.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And then, she decided to become a seafarer.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, we do all that we can to attract young talent into the maritime sector.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There are five more Members who have raised their hands.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am trying to get to all of you, so do yourselves justice and to others.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Just a quick question on the status on the autonomous vehicle trials.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Other than the Punggol one, there is one more that is running in Marina Bay and Shenton Way area.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Just to have an update on the progress of that.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Also, it is a busy area, how will we deal with traffic congestion if there are some issues with the trials?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I mentioned the two bus numbers which has now slipped my memory.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman
text: He mentioned about the shared space of motorcycles on the road.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman
text: There are 140,000 motorcycles, if I got it right, and there are 70,000 motorcycles from the causeway that goes to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman
text: Almost half of them come from the other side.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman
text: And yet, they do not pay any COE, they do not pay any road tax.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman
text: How do we justify Singaporeans paying so much, sharing the same space, and yet the other side are not doing so?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, first of all, I have a lot of sympathy for the concern.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We hear this a lot, very often from our Singaporean motorcycle riders.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As to whether or not they are being treated fairly.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: This is why we have the Vehicle Entry Permit (VEP) and the Goods Vehicle Permit (GVP) schemes.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The idea is that Malaysian motorbikes, when they come in, they pay a fee and then this equalises the cost.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The fees are set such that the cost of owning and using a foreign registered vehicle in Singapore is equalised with that of a Singaporean vehicle.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We applied a fee to cars, we apply a similar but lower fee to motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: At the same time as when the RTS Link is open.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: In addition, for our local motorcycles, just so that I address this point, the Government already applies lower ARF, lower road taxes – in fact, ERP charges are also lower for motorcycles relative to other vehicle types.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, it addresses and recognises how motorcycles are in fact using not fully the same road space as a car but nonetheless still using some road space.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: They cause some level of congestion and therefore, we have to make sure that is priced properly and the externalities are properly taken into account.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But he would appreciate that time is not the only factor contributing to a good commuting experience.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: A one-hour plus commute standing all the way is not easy on the back and the legs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And since the binding constraint as Senior Minister of State Sun said, is not buses, but bus captains, can LTA deploy more double decker buses or bendy buses on heavily utilised routes, especially during peak hours, so that commuters can get a seat during their commute, or minimally do not miss their bus because it is full.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think our intent is to try to deploy as many double decker buses as possible.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Just to explain a little bit, we do still have a legacy fleet of single deck buses.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I am often asked, "Oh, why is it during peak hour, we are still deploying single deck buses?" and I get lots of angry emails very often on this particular issue.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The reason is actually there are additions to the buses.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I put in all my double deckers and then, on top of that, during peak hour, whatever single deckers I have, I also put in.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And therefore, people do not like it when they see the single deck bus coming, but it is in fact an addition; it is not a subtraction.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And in Singapore, because we have to customise our buses, we had to wait for some time before the double deck electric buses came on stream.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And so in the interim we did buy some of the single deck electric buses to start the electrification process.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, these are sort of the reasons that are hard to see on the outside, but I hope the Member and the public understands why you still see single decks on the roads today.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: Given the multiple road diversions and traffic disruptions that residents along the North-South corridor construction zone have had to endure since 2020, including the ongoing closure of Marymount Flyover and the successive road reconfiguration in the Bishan-Sin Ming area, what is the current construction timeline for the tunnel section of the North-South corridor from Lentor Avenue to the city?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: And what measures is LTA taking to minimise further disruption to residents and road users for the remaining construction period leading up to 2029?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: I welcome efforts to also normalise asking for a seat on buses and trains, especially for seniors, pregnant women and those with less visible conditions.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: Encouraging commuters to communicate their needs can help to build a more gracious and responsive public transport culture.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: At the same time, we have seen incidents overseas where disputes over priority seating escalated into confrontations, such as the case in Taiwan, when a woman calmly handed over her shopping bag to a fellow commuter and then proceeded to kick an elderly woman across the aisle just as the elderly woman was demanding that the younger woman give up her seat.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And we continue to seek our residents' patience and understanding.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Just bear in mind that we are trying to enhance transport connectivity at the end of the day, as well as to shorten travel times for our commuters as well as our motorists.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Before the commencement of construction works, the LTA often carries out assessments to determine if existing road networks can be improved.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: LTA and its contractors will also work closely with stakeholders and residents living near the works to minimise the inconvenience caused to them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And where possible, additional road or lane closures which are needed during certain phases of work will be carried out during off peak periods to avoid further inconvenience to residents.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We are quite close to guillotine time, so the last two clarifications.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Sorry, Minister of State Baey, I forgot the second part.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Yes, I thank Ms Chen for the clarification.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Indeed, to make our commuting experience enjoyable, pleasant, every commuter plays a role.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Therefore, whether is it someone who needs help or can offer help, we want to make this a norm that people are encouraged to ask for a seat, you know, and it is not just for priority seats.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Any seats could be taken or could be given up for anyone who is in greater need.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: And we will continue in these efforts to cultivate a gracious and a caring culture on public transport.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We hope that through education we can develop a new generation of commuters.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: And the kids can also influence their parents and elders to be more thoughtful for other commuters.

speaker: The Chairman
text: With the Singapore Kindness Movement, let us all be kinder.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I am not sure that my cut on covered linkways for condominiums has been adequately addressed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Could I just ask for Minister of State to address the questions specifically regarding those situations where the condominium needs assistance for a covered linkway, including in a no man's land situation to connect them to the nearest bus stop?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: And also my suggestion that URA and LTA mandate at the planning permission stage that developers provide shelter connectivity to the nearest public transport node?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I know that for existing condominiums or estates that were built before this requirement, there could be challenges.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: And for LTA's planning, you might be aware that we already provide linkways, covered linkways within transport nodes, 400 metres, 800 metres within Friendly Streets and all these.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: But in areas where the land belongs to another agency, like PUB as in the case that he mentioned in his cut, LTA will help to discuss with the different stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: If it is on PUB land, PUB must give approval.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: And we have to respect the authorities' assessment of the land.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: There could be drainage or water pipes underneath that may be affected if we have to dig and build a sheltered linkway.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, there are technical considerations that we have to respect in the respective agency's assessment.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I know the Member has been pushing for a particular condominium, Parc Vera, if I am not wrong.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: These are things that would need to be worked through.

speaker: The Chairman
text: On that note, can I invite Ms Tin if you would like to withdraw your amendment?
